News from the US, Europe, Asia Pacific, Africa, Middle East, America</description><link>https://www.france24.com/en/</link><lastBuildDate>Sat, 07 Nov 2026 10:45:50 GMT</lastBuildDate><atom:link href="https://www.france24.com/en/rss" rel="self" type="application/rss+xml"/><item><category>France</category><title>French 2027 presidential elections: How Mélenchon became a Gen Z favourite</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261107-french-2027-presidential-elections-how-m%C3%A9lenchon-became-a-gen-z-favourite</link><description>

Three weeks after undergoing surgery for lung cancer, Pope Francis has begun a three-nation tour of Latin America, saying he felt better than he looked. His first stop is Uruguay, the continent’s most secular country. Jack Pownall reports.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/b2ce00a4-da8e-11f1-a2d2-695cb59fade5/w:1024/p:16x9/EN-20261107-101157-101324-CS.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/b2ce00a4-da8e-11f1-a2d2-695cb59fade5/w:1024/p:16x9/EN-20261107-101157-101324-CS.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">b8150620-da8e-11f1-801f-71870b021f26</guid><pubDate>Sat, 07 Nov 2026 09:41:23 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>FRANCE24</dc:creator></item><item><category></category><title>AI Data centres face growing backlash</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/ai-data-centres-face-growing-backlash</link><description>

</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/7b12b7e0-da8e-11f1-96c8-d18c5759e759/w:1024/p:16x9/EN-20261107-100946-101139-CS.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/7b12b7e0-da8e-11f1-96c8-d18c5759e759/w:1024/p:16x9/EN-20261107-100946-101139-CS.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">80584c60-da8e-11f1-af87-a90c70a6f21e</guid><pubDate>Sat, 07 Nov 2026 09:39:55 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>FRANCE24</dc:creator></item><item><category></category><title>Yemen: 30 dead in strikes on Taiz market</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/yemen-30-dead-in-strikes-on-taiz-market</link><description>
At least 30 people have reportedly been killed in an attack on a market in Yemen’s Taiz province, with Houthi rebels blaming Saudi airstrikes. Government forces and local authorities have disputed the claim, instead accusing the Houthis of indiscriminate fire. The province has witnessed intense clashes in recent weeks and is home to around half of the more than 300,000 people displaced by the latest fighting. Caroline Baum reports.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/9da14e8a-da8d-11f1-9c90-bf1914cabd52/w:1024/p:16x9/EN-20261107-090700-090851-CS.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/9da14e8a-da8d-11f1-9c90-bf1914cabd52/w:1024/p:16x9/EN-20261107-090700-090851-CS.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">a297adee-da8d-11f1-b71c-09c09631d97d</guid><pubDate>Sat, 07 Nov 2026 09:37:16 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>FRANCE24</dc:creator></item><item><category></category><title>USA: Democrats vow to investigate Donald Trump</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/usa-democrats-vow-to-investigate-donald-trump</link><description>

A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from California's Vandenberg Space Force Base this evening (Nov. 6) at 7:48 p.m. EST (4:48 p.m. local California time; 0048 GMT on Nov. 7), rising into the sky as the sun sank toward the Pacific.

The launch kicked off the USSF-432 mission for the U.S. Space Force, which we know little about. Neither SpaceX nor the Space Force told us much about USSF-432 beforehand, and we learned tonight; SpaceX cut its webcast off about 10 minutes into the flight, shortly after the Falcon 9's first stage came back to Earth for a landing.

That touchdown occurred aboard the SpaceX droneship "Of Course I Still Love You," which was stationed downrange in the Pacific Ocean. It wrapped up the eighth flight for this particular booster, which is designated 1095.

The Falcon 9's upper stage, meanwhile, continued carrying its mystery payload skyward. It could be headed to low Earth orbit, outside observers speculate.

"It is possibly a batch of classified LEO satellites for the USSF's Space Based Sensing and Targeting (SBST) portfolio based on SpaceX's Starshield satellite bus, based on locations of rocket stage drop zones being exact fits with previous Starlink Group 15 launches," NextSpaceflight.com wrote in a mission description.

Starlink is SpaceX's LEO broadband megaconstellation, which consists of more than 11,000 active satellites. Starshield is a similar system designed to provide services to the U.S. military and its allies. Starshield satellites are believed to be based heavily on the Starlink spacecraft bus.

Previous Booster 1095 missions

GPS-III 8 | 6 Starlink missions

USSF-432 was the 119th Falcon 9 launch of 2026, and the 14th national-security flight of the rocket so far this year. The vast majority of Falcon 9 missions in 2026 — more than 70% — have been devoted to building out the Starlink megaconstellation.

SpaceX has also launched six other missions this year. Three were operational flights of the company's Falcon Heavy rocket, while the other three were test missions of its next-gen Starship vehicle. SpaceX plans to retire both the Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy shortly after the fully reusable Starship, the biggest and most powerful rocket ever built, is up and running.

]]> <![CDATA[ On this day in space! Nov. 6, 1572: A German astronomer discovers the Tycho supernova with the naked eye, but everyone thought the cosmic explosion was a 'new star' ]]>

On Nov. 6, 1572, the German astronomer Wolfgang Schulër observed a supernova with his bare eyes. He spotted the exploding star in the constellation Cassiopeia. It was as bright as Venus and could even be seen during the day.

Astronomers were really confused, because it looked like a star just appeared out of nowhere. Schulër may have been the first to see it, but the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe is widely credited for the discovery. Brahe studied it in detail and wrote a whole book about this so-called "new star." It then became known as "Tycho's Star."

At the time, supernovas had not yet been discovered. Tycho's Star was finally classified as a supernova in the 1940s. Scientists now think it was a small star called a white dwarf that exploded thousands of years ago. Because Tycho's Star is 13,000 light-years from Earth, it took a while before anyone could see it.

Why it mattered

The Tycho supernova, known technically as SN 1572, is known today as a Type Ia supernova, which is a star explosion in a binary star system in which a white dwarf star draws material away from its partner, then explodes. But in 1572, the Tycho supernova appeared as something very different: a bright new star.

While Schulër was first, other astronomers also observed the apparently new star in the sky. Tycho Brahe's numerous observations are the most well known, in no small part becuause he wrote a book all about them in "De Stella Nova" (Latin for "On The New Star." At the time, the prevailing theory among scientists was that the stars were unchanging, yet here was a new star -- a changed sky.

"The 16th century exploding star, which appeared in the constellation Cassiopeia, was seen in daylight for about two weeks, and remained visible to the naked eye for 16 months," the University of California Berkeley wrote in 2004. "Brahe's meticulous record of the brightening and dimming of the supernova now allows astronomers to identify its 'light signature" as that of a Type Ia supernova."

"This was at the end of the Dark Ages in Europe, and these observations were an important piece of evidence that the heavens were not immutable," astronomer Alex Filippenko, who led a 2004 study on the origins of the Tycho supernova, said at the time.

Today, astronomers are closely watching another star that might explode. Called T Corona Borealis, or the Blaze Star, the object is expected to be on the verge of exploding in a nova (a star explosion that is smaller than a supernova and may not destroy the star). is one of 11 known stars observed to have recurring nova explosions within gaps of 100 years or so.

]]> <![CDATA[ AST SpaceMobile announces new 'Blacklift' rocket, targets 2028 launch debut ]]> Another new private rocket is in the works.

AST SpaceMobile announced today (Nov. 6) that it's building a reusable rocket called Blacklift to launch its broadband satellites to low Earth orbit (LEO), with first flight targeted in 2028.

The news comes just 10 days after Cowboy Space unveiled Big Iron, a rocket designed to launch its constellation of 20,000 AI data centers. Cowboy Space is also targeting 2028 for its first liftoff.

"The Blacklift rocket is the springboard to significantly expand our total addressable market, providing AST SpaceMobile with regular unconstrained access to orbit and providing for most favorable owners’ economics in the industry," Abel Avellan, the company's founder, chairman and CEO, said in a statement today.

"This will accelerate our mission to build a new layer of global connectivity, extending connectivity beyond terrestrial networks and helping to bring AI-enabled services wherever people live, work and travel," Avellan added.

Texas-based AST SpaceMobile is building a LEO constellation composed of its BlueBird satellites, which beam internet service directly to cell phones. The company has launched 13 BlueBirds to date, including eight "Block 2" variants. The antennas on each of these next-gen spacecraft cover a whopping 2,400 square feet (223 square m) — the largest ever deployed in LEO by a commercial satellite.

BlueBirds have flown atop three different rockets to date — SpaceX's Falcon 9, Blue Origin's New Glenn and India's Launch Vehicle Mark-3. But AST SpaceMobile wants to get more vertically integrated, which explains the push to develop Blacklift.

The company won't be starting from scratch. It has signed a deal with another Texas-based outfit, Firefly Aerospace, to provide the engines (and associated engineering services) for the first three Blacklift launches. After that, AST SpaceMobile will build the engines itself, under a licensing agreement with Firefly.

Those engines are Miranda, which will power Blacklift's booster, and Vira, which will power the upper stage.

Neither engine has flight experience. (Firefly's currently operational rocket, Alpha, uses Reavers in its booster and Lightnings in its upper stage.) But Miranda has been tested extensively on the ground, firing for more than 4,200 seconds over the course of 175 hot fires, according to AST SpaceMobile.

"The Miranda engine will allow us to leapfrog the traditional five-to-10-year development cycle as we build Blacklift," AST SpaceMobile President Scott Wisniewski said in the same statement.

The "supply and services" agreement for the first three launches is worth $500 million. The licensing agreement cost AST SpaceMobile about $800 million, with half of that paid in cash and half in stock, according to the statement.

Blacklift will be able to haul 20 tons to LEO. Each launch will therefore be able to loft up to five BlueBird satellites, according to today's announcement. (For perspective: The Falcon 9's LEO lift capacity is about 25 tons.)

BlueBirds will continue going up while AST SpaceMobile gets Blacklift ready to fly: The company already holds contracts with other providers to launch more than 100 of the satellites over the course of 2027 and 2028.

The launch landscape will likely be very different when Blacklift, Big Iron and other new rockets come online. SpaceX has said that it plans to phase out the Falcon 9, as well as its Falcon Heavy heavy lifter, after its Starship megarocket gets up and running.

That milestone could come in the next few years, ushering in something of a launch crunch for satellite operators. SpaceX has indicated that it will prioritize launches of its own satellites with Starship. And there will be a lot of them to loft — 100,000 Starlink V3 satellites and a million Starmind AI data centers, company founder and CEO Elon Musk has suggested.

]]> <![CDATA[ What's that bright 'star' in the early morning sky? It's not a star at all! ]]> Early morning risers heading to work or school before sunrise are likely to notice a very bright, star-like object appearing low in the east-southeast sky just before sunrise. What is somewhat amazing is that just a couple of weeks ago this object wasn't there at all, but now it literally stands out with such brilliance as to almost command the attention of commuters who might be traveling in an easterly direction to "Look at me!"

The object in question is, of course, the planet Venus, which is currently amid one of its most spectacular forays into the morning sky, literally "vaulting up" into prominence.

]]> <![CDATA[ You can see another galaxy with the naked eye — here's how to find it ]]> The first time I showed someone the Andromeda galaxy (M31), our conversation did not go quite as planned.

I'd carefully worked my way across the sky, starting from the Great Square of Pegasus and hopping from star to star until I was confident I had the right patch. I pointed the telescope, got M31 in its crosshairs and proudly announced to my wife that I had found the closest giant galaxy to the Milky Way. Would she like to see it?

She then stayed quiet for a little too long as she looked through the eyepiece. Then came an unexpected question. "Is it near that little smudge?" Hmmm. "Err, no. It is that little smudge," I replied.

There was a pause. Of course, I knew exactly what had happened. We'd both seen photographs of M31 — a vast spiral galaxy with a brilliant center, sweeping dust lanes and hundreds of billions of stars. What we were actually looking at was a grayish blur that could easily have been mistaken for a mark on the eyepiece.

That apparent disappointment is now my favorite part of finding Andromeda because the unimpressive smudge is real. The light entering your eyes has been traveling across space for about 2.5 million years. No screen, photograph or telescope is necessary. You are intercepting ancient light in your backyard. Technically, the Triangulum Galaxy (M33), about 2.7 million light-years away, can be seen with the naked eye, so it is therefore the most distant object the naked eye can see. But not mine — I've never seen it. M31 is a much more realistic naked-eye target.

What's happening and when to look

Early November is an excellent time to find M31 from the Northern Hemisphere. It's high and well placed during the evening, and this week the moon is becoming particularly cooperative. New Moon falls around Nov. 9, giving us several evenings with little or no moonlight to wash out faint deep-sky objects.

I usually begin with the star Alpheratz, one of the corner stars of the Great Square of Pegasus. You go two stars left, two stars up, and you arrive at M31. Another route — and a good way to check you're in the right place — starts in Cassiopeia, the distinctive W-shaped constellation high in the northeastern sky on autumn evenings. You can use its second V-shape as an arrow pointing straight at M31.

You can do that star-hop with the naked eye or a pair of binoculars, but M31 is visible to the naked eye only under a very dark sky. However, don't look for a miniature version of the photographs. Expect a faint, elongated patch with a slightly brighter middle.

There's another beginner trap to avoid. Images make Andromeda look compact, but its full apparent extent is enormous — several times the width of the full moon — and our eyes usually pick up only the much brighter central region. Once you know that, the smudge starts making more sense.

I'm going to look for Andromeda this week in the least heroic way possible. No expedition. No mountain-top observing location. No elaborate equipment. I'll wait until it is properly dark, step outside and then use Cassiopeia and the stars of Andromeda to work my way toward M31. I'll then reach for my 10x50 binoculars, which are rarely far from my side after dark, whether I'm at home or traveling. They gather enough light to make the galaxy's bright central region much more obvious without turning the exercise into a technical one.

A really useful skill here — whether looking unaided or through binoculars — is averted vision. Instead of staring directly at the galaxy, look slightly beside it. The more light-sensitive parts of the retina away from the center of our vision can make faint objects easier to detect. It feels slightly ridiculous the first time you do it — deliberately not looking at the thing you're trying to see — but it works.

If light pollution means you need binoculars, that still counts. No one gets a prize for detecting Andromeda unaided. After all, the extraordinary part isn't how you see it. It's what the light has done before reaching you. When those photons began their journey, modern humans did not exist. They crossed intergalactic space for roughly 2.5 million years and ended their trip in your retina. Stargazing is often described as looking back in time. With Andromeda, that phrase stops being a metaphor.

Stargazer's corner: November 6-12, 2026

This is the week you've been waiting for if you want to spend time on faint objects rather than fighting moonlight. Without a bright moon overhead, spend some time on Andromeda, but revisit the Double Cluster in Perseus (NGC 869 and NGC 884). Binoculars show it beautifully, and unlike M31, it becomes more obviously crowded with stars as you increase magnification. Two other large, bright open star clusters in this region that look great in 10x50 binoculars are the glittering stars of NGC 752 in Andromeda and M34, a bright, hazy patch in Perseus.

Also keep an eye out for "shooting stars" because the Northern Taurid meteor shower peaks overnight on Nov. 11-12. Rates are low — around five meteors per hour under ideal conditions — so don't expect them to "light up the night sky". But they can produce bright, long-lasting 'fireballs' that can add a bit of pizzazz to a stargazing session.

Now that you've found its jewel, the Andromeda galaxy, it's worth trying to construct the constellation itself. As with M31, start with the Great Square of Pegasus and Alpheratz at its northeastern corner. Although it looks like part of the square, Alpheratz actually belongs to Andromeda. From Alpheratz, follow a curving line of stars away from the square through Mirach and on toward Almach. That gives you the basic shape of Andromeda — not the easiest constellation to imagine as a mythological princess, but a useful chain of stars to learn.

]]> <![CDATA[ Giant exoplanet emerges from the dark when the James Webb Space Telescope turns out the starlight ]]> Sometimes science can seem really counter-intuitive. For example, occasionally in astronomy, you can see more with less light. Case in point: the emergence of a giant planet in observations made by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), when astronomers found a way to block out light from the planet's parent star.

The extrasolar planet, or exoplanet, in question is 51 Eridani b (51 ERI b), a gas giant with the same mass as around 11 Jupiters that orbits a star located around 97 light-years away. 51 ERI b was discovered back in 2015 by ground-based telescopes, but the planet was missing from observations of the system made by the JWST. That wasn't a failing of the JWST itself; no one is doubting the observing capabilities of the most powerful telescope humanity has ever hoisted into orbit around Earth. Instead, it was a result of starlight from the star 51 ERI A obscuring this intimidatingly massive world.

The brightest planets are 100,000 times fainter than their host stars, meaning spotting them is like observing a firefly hovering around a lighthouse. Even using a tool called a coronagraph to block the star isn't enough to reveal the planet, as that doesn't stop all the starlight.

The only solution to this glaring problem is a computer program to wipe out the starlight.

"For the past 20 years, astronomers have tackled this problem by observing a different star and using its image as a reference," Jason Wang of Northwestern University explained in a statement. "Then, they subtract that reference image from the original observation to remove the unwanted glare to reveal faint planets that otherwise might be hidden."

There is a problem with this process, however. Even the most stable telescopes "wobble." For instance, the JWST requires cryocoolers to keep its NIRCam instrument super cold, and those coolers have little motors that can cause the mirrors to vibrate. This movement, however slight, causes a scatter in starlight.

The result is enough glare remaining to obscure a planet, but Wang and colleagues developed a new approach to this problem.

Telescopes their more stable digital twins

The new approach taken by the team is dubbed Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets (FLIP), and it involves creating a digital "twin" of a telescope. Essentially a virtual replica that simulates how starlight travels through the telescope's mirrors and reaches its detectors.

This twin is then fine-tuned to account for millions of tiny imperfections in the original telescope. The digital twin is then tweaked until it aligns with observations from the actual telescope. Astronomers can then remove the simulated glare from the original image.

To assess the validity of the technique, the researchers took a second look at JWST observations of two star systems with known exoplanets, HIP 65426 and 51 Eridani, and one system, TYC 5899, with no known planets.

The researchers found that, in terms of detecting faint exoplanets, FLIP outperformed conventional image-processing techniques two to 15 times. This led to ERI b emerging from data collected by the JWST two years ago.

"We showed that we can actually recover a planet that people previously couldn't see," Wang said. "This is real data in a real scenario. It was science left on the table because we didn’t have the right tools to analyze the data in the most optimal way."

The team hopes that FLIP can now be adopted by other astronomers in a bid to recover hitherto undiscovered exoplanets that have been hidden by the glare of their stars.

This could be a major boon for NASA's proposed Habitable Worlds Observatory, which aims to directly photograph Earth-like planets orbiting distant sun-like stars.

"We know of no planets around other stars that are like those in our own solar system," team leader Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez of Northwestern University said. "It's not that they don’t exist. It's that we cannot see them.

The change is a result of the fact that Dimporphos is now traveling at around 2.7 millimeters per second more slowly than it did before the collision.

The changes caused by DART were small. But in a real Earth-threatening scenario, even such a tiny shift could help divert an asteroid on a collision course — as long as scientists get enough advance warning of its approach.

   <description>Zase přišel ten čas, kdy se říjen slavil v listopadu – samozřejmě ten Velký. Krkonoše ohlásily první opravdovou bílou nadílku a tamní horská služba se radovala, že dostala tři nové sněžné skútry. A že se ochlazovalo, určitě někomu přišla vhod zpráva o tom, že brandýský Kovopodnik inovoval a víc než zdvojnásobil pětačtyřicetimilimetrovou izolaci maringotek, které monopolně vyráběl. Republiku potrápily mlhy – a nejen ji; taky západoněmeckého pilota, který po ztrátě orientace omylem přeletěl hranici a nouzově přistál u Holušic na Strakonicku.</description>

   <title>Právníci kritizují dětský certifikát: Se záměrem souhlasíme, s provedením ne</title>
   <link>https://www.denik.cz/cesko/cesko-detsky-certifikat-kritizuji-pravnici-proc/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=feed-vse&utm_campaign=ceskolipsky.denik.cz&utm_content=cesko</link>
   <description>Dětský certifikát, tedy evidence skutečností důležitých pro práci s dětmi, je zvláštní výpis z rejstříku trestů, jenž má zabránit práci s dětmi osobám odsouzeným za vybrané závažné trestné činy. Stát jej zavádí jako preventivní nástroj na ochranu dětí, protože dosavadní zákazy práce s dětmi byly časově omezené a ne vždy dokázaly zabránit návratu rizikových osob do profesí, kde přicházejí do kontaktu s nezletilými. Dětský certifikát byl načten do novely trestního zákoníku jako pozměňovací návrh skupiny poslanců napříč politickými stranami. Kritikům se nelíbí některé nedodělky a nelogičnosti v zákoně nebo to, že neměří „stejným metrem“. Dodávají ale, že s principe m dětského certifikátu souhlasí, připomínky mají pouze k provedení. Některá opatření kritizuje i současný ministr spravedlnosti Jeroným Tejc (za ANO) či bývalá ministryně spravedlnosti Eva Decroix (ODS).</description>

]]> Okresní kolo ČEPS Cupu – florbal 1. stupeň základních škol (kluci) 2026/2027 https://www.vybezek.eu/296441-okresni-kolo-ceps-cupu-florbal-1-stupen-zakladnich-skol-kluci-2026-2027/ Thu, 05 Nov 2026 09:35:41 +0000 https://www.vybezek.eu/?p=296441 Ve středu 4. listopadu 2026 se ve Varnsdorfu ve sportovní hale hrál florbal, proběhlo okresní kolo ČEPS Cupu Děčín-Šluknovsko pro 1. stupeň základních škol (kluci).

Ve středu 4. listopadu 2026 se ve sportovní hale ve Varnsdorfu uskutečnilo okresní kolo florbalového turnaje ČEPS Cupu, určeného pro žáky 1.–5. tříd základních škol.

Turnaj se hrál systémem 3 + 1. Každý tým se utkal s každým soupeřem dvoukolově, přičemž jedno utkání trvalo 2 × 8 minut. Na turnaji se představily tři týmy – ZŠ Východní, Centrum dětí a mládeže Česká Kamenice a naše škola. Každý tým tak odehrál celkem čtyři utkání. Vítězný tým turnaje postoupí do krajského finále.

Hned v úvodním utkání nás čekal nejtěžší soupeř, domácí ZŠ Východní. Po velmi vyrovnaném a bojovném průběhu jsme dokázali zvítězit těsným výsledkem 4:3. Druhý zápas proti soupeři z České Kamenice jsme zvládli výborně a po přesvědčivém výkonu jsme zvítězili 6:2. Ve druhém kole jsme se znovu utkali se ZŠ Východní. Tentokrát nám soupeř porážku oplatil a po dramatickém průběhu jsme prohráli nejtěsnějším rozdílem 2:3. Jelikož i ZŠ Východní zvítězila nad Českou Kamenicí, bylo před závěrečným utkáním jasné, že o vítězi turnaje rozhodne počet vstřelených branek proti tomuto soupeři.

Do závěrečného utkání jsme proto nastoupili s jasnou taktikou – vstřelit co nejvíce branek. Po většinu turnaje nás v brance skvěle držel Adam Reichert, který několika výbornými zákroky podržel tým v nejtěžších chvílích. Pro rozhodující utkání jsme však zvolili odvážný taktický tah. Adama jsme přesunuli z branky do pole, protože sehraná trojice Adam Reichert, Hugo Bláha a Dominik Košín měla za úkol nastřílet co nejvíce gólů. Tento plán dokonale vyšel. Našemu týmu se podařilo zvítězit vysokým rozdílem a vstřelit soupeři 13 branek, tedy o tři více, než dokázala ZŠ Východní. Díky lepšímu skóre jsme se stali vítězi okresního kola a vybojovali si zasloužený postup do krajského finále.

Velkou pochvalu si zaslouží celý tým za bojovnost, nasazení a kolektivní výkon. V našem týmu nastoupila také jediná dívka Barča Šeráková, která byla velmi platnou hráčkou a svým výkonem významně přispěla k celkovému úspěchu. Z individuálních výkonů bych chtěla vyzdvihnout Huga Bláhu, Adama Reicherta, Maxe Zachariáše a Dominika Košína, kteří patřili k oporám našeho týmu. Poděkování však patří všem hráčům za výbornou reprezentaci školy.
